title: A 20-year study examining the effects of salmon lice on the return rate, time at sea, and marine growth of sea trout migrating from the river Shieldaig in Scotland
content:
Abstract
The intensive rearing of Atlantic salmon in open net pens has led to concerns that fish farms can increase environmental numbers of the salmon louse, Lepeophtheirus salmonis, to the detriment of wild sea trout Salmo trutta populations. Here, we examine the marine growth, time at sea, and return rates of trout in relation to sea lice infestation pressure. The study was conducted between 1999 and 2020 at a permanent fish trap located near the mouth of the river Shieldaig, which opens to Loch Torridon on the West coast of Scotland. During the study, the wild trout population of the river was supplemented by stocking with hatchery-origin fish (fish reared in a hatchery and marked by removal of the adipose fin). Sea trout emigrating as smolts and returning to the study river were caught by the trap, identified using Passive Integrated Transponder tags and measured to determine their marine growth, time at sea and return rates. The prevalence of lice infested sea trout surveyed in the area below the trap was used as a proxy metric to characterise the infestation pressure that fish were exposed to during their marine migrations. As lice infestation pressure increased, so the specific growth rate of the returning fish caught by the trap declined. There was no evidence that time at sea was affected by lice infestation pressure. Wild-origin fish had a greater return rate than hatchery-origin fish at all levels of lice infestation pressure, with the difference increasing with increasing pressure. There was strong evidence of a decrease in return rates for hatchery-origin fish as lice infestation pressure increased, but this effect was not significant for wild-origin fish. The negative impacts of high lice infestation are likely to have adverse consequences for the fecundity of the returning Shieldaig sea trout population. The observed differences between the return rates of the wild-origin and hatchery-origin fish demonstrated that, while fish of hatchery-origin, marked by removal of an adipose fin, may increase the power of a study to detect the effect of an environmental pressure, caution should be employed when using these fish to quantify impact.
